items.prompt: Two classmates hear the same true bake-sale numbers. One stays calm and the other panics. What best explains this?
choices: Each of them brought different knowledge and stakes to the numbers
One of them must have been told slightly different numbers
The panicking one simply listened with less care than the other
items.explanation: The facts were identical. The reaction differs because each reader filters the facts through what they already know and what they care about.

items.prompt: Which of these is a fact about a message rather than an effect of it?
choices: The principal felt alarmed on hearing about it
The groupmate found the update reassuring
The sale raised $340 of its $500 goal
items.explanation: Facts are what is true and checkable. Feelings and reactions are effects, and they belong to the reader.

items.prompt: Which of these is an effect of a message rather than a fact in it?
choices: The rain forced the sale to move indoors
The reader ends up worried about the field trip
The make-up sale is planned for this Saturday
items.explanation: An effect is what the message does to a particular reader. The rain and the Saturday plan are facts that were true before anyone read anything.

items.prompt: A message contains only true statements. Does that guarantee it lands well?
choices: No, a true message can still alarm or confuse a reader
Yes, because truth always produces the intended reaction
Yes, as long as the message is also kept very short
items.explanation: Truth is necessary but not sufficient. What gets foregrounded and what the reader already knows also shape the reaction.

items.prompt: Who controls the facts of a message, and who partly controls its effect?
choices: The reader controls the facts; the writer controls the effect entirely
Neither person controls anything once the message has been sent
The writer controls the facts; the reader's situation shapes the effect
items.explanation: The writer decides what is true and what is stated. The effect depends on the writer's choices combined with the reader's knowledge and stakes.

items.prompt: The bake sale update reassures your groupmate but alarms the principal. Did the facts change between them?
choices: Yes, the principal must have received a worse set of facts
No, the facts stayed the same and only the readers differed
Yes, the groupmate must have received the better numbers
items.explanation: Same facts, different readers, different effects. That gap is exactly what audience awareness manages.

items.prompt: Which statement about facts and effect is correct?
choices: They are two separate things that do not move together
They always move together, so true means well received
They are the same thing described with two names
items.explanation: Facts are about what is true; effect is about how it lands. A message can be perfect on one and poor on the other.

items.prompt: Why can the same sentence reassure one person and worry another?
choices: One of the two people is probably misreading the words
Sentences have no stable meaning for any reader at all
People read it against their own background and duties
items.explanation: Meaning depends partly on the reader. Someone who saw the rain and someone hearing secondhand start from very different places.

items.prompt: A baker tells a regular customer 'we ran out of bread by noon' and the customer smiles. The same line makes a new supplier frown. What is the best reading?
choices: The baker must have told the supplier a different story
The customer reads it as popularity, the supplier as lost sales
The customer misunderstood the sentence and the supplier did not
The baker's words changed meaning between the two listeners
items.explanation: The words are identical. Each listener supplies a different frame, so one hears good news and the other hears a problem.
items.reference:
Facts

What's true

Effect

How it lands on THIS reader

Why: the same true statement can build trust with one reader and alarm another — truth and effect are separate axes.

A message carries two separate things at once. They don't move together.

FactsEffect
NatureFixed, checkableDepends on the reader

Common mistake

Treating a bad reaction as proof something false was said, or a good reaction as proof the message was complete. Neither follows — accuracy and effect are graded separately.
items.reflection: Think of a time the same true news made one person calm and another upset. What did each of them already know or care about that the other did not?

items.prompt: Mia says, 'The party was loud and ended early.' Her friend laughs; her landlord is upset. A classmate concludes Mia must have lied to one of them. What is wrong with that conclusion?
choices: Identical true words can produce different effects on different readers
Nothing, since a different reaction always signals a different story
It is wrong only because landlords do not care about parties
It is wrong only because the party happened to be on a weekend
items.explanation: A different reaction is not evidence of different facts. It is evidence of different readers, which is the whole point of separating facts from effect.

items.prompt: You told two people the same true thing and both reacted badly. Which response keeps facts and effect on separate axes?
choices: Re-check the facts, since a bad reaction means a false statement
Repeat the same words more slowly until both react well
Apologize to both and say you will never mention it again
Check what each reader needed first, then adjust emphasis and detail
items.explanation: Since the facts were true, the fix lives on the effect side: what was foregrounded, what was missing, and what the reader needed to settle.

items.prompt: Which three lenses does every reader filter a message through?
choices: Speed, length, and spelling of the message
Context, incentives, and channel expectations
Tone, volume, and font style of the message
items.explanation: The unit's three lenses are what the reader already knows, what they care about, and what the medium trains them to expect.

items.prompt: Which lens asks, 'What does this reader already know?'
choices: Context
Incentives
Channel expectations
items.explanation: Context is the background the reader holds before your message arrives.

items.prompt: Which lens asks, 'What is this reader responsible for or judged on?'
choices: Context
Channel expectations
Incentives
items.explanation: Incentives are what the reader cares about, answers for, or will be judged on.

items.prompt: Which lens asks, 'What does this format make the reader expect?'
choices: Context
Channel
Incentives
items.explanation: A text, an email, and a school announcement each set different expectations before a word is read.

items.prompt: Your groupmate watched the rain happen. Which lens does that fact belong to?
choices: Context, because they already know what happened
Incentives, because they care about the outcome
Channel, because they were present in person
items.explanation: What someone already knows from being there is their context.

items.prompt: Your teacher is accountable for the $500. Which lens does that belong to?
choices: Context, because they know the goal exists
Channel, because they received a note
Incentives, because it is what they answer for
items.explanation: Being accountable for an outcome is an incentive. It decides what they will fixate on.

items.prompt: Do the three lenses act one after another or all at once?
choices: One after another, starting with context
All at once, on the same message
Only one applies to any given message
items.explanation: Every message is filtered by all three lenses simultaneously, whether or not the writer accounts for them.

items.prompt: A text to a friend and a school-wide announcement say the same thing. Which lens explains why they read differently?
choices: Channel
Context
Incentives
items.explanation: The format sets how casual or official the message feels before the reader processes any content.

items.prompt: Your neighbor, who is also on the building committee, hears that the elevator is broken. Their first question is 'Who is paying for the repair?' Which lens predicts this?
choices: Context, since they already know the elevator exists
Channel, since the news arrived by casual hallway chat
Incentives, since they answer for the building's budget
Incentives, since the elevator belongs to the building
items.explanation: A committee member is judged on money and decisions, so that is what they fixate on. Knowing the elevator exists is background, not the driver.
items.reference:
🧠 Context — what do they already know?
🎯 Incentives — what do they personally care about?
📡 Channel — what does the medium train them to expect?

Why: every reader filters a message through all three lenses at once, whether the writer accounts for it or not.

Writing 'for everyone' usually means tuning for none of the three lenses well: over-explaining to someone with context, under-explaining to someone without it, wrong register for the channel.
items.reflection: Pick someone you will message this week. What do they already know, what are they responsible for, and what does your chosen medium lead them to expect?

items.prompt: A coach gets the same short text from a player's parent and from the player's teammate: 'Can't make it Saturday.' Only the parent adds an apology and an explanation. Which lens most plausibly drives the difference?
choices: Context differs because the teammate is less informed
Channel expectations differ between the two senders
Incentives differ because the teammate wants to skip
Facts differ, since the parent was told a longer story
items.explanation: A parent writing to a coach expects a more formal register than one teammate writing to another. The medium and relationship set the norm.

items.prompt: A message is too detailed for one reader and too thin for another. Which diagnosis fits best?
choices: The two readers differ on context, so detail landed differently
The writer failed the facts lens for both readers equally
The two readers must have received it through different channels
The writer chose the wrong font for the shorter note
items.explanation: More detail helps the reader missing background and burdens the reader who already has it, so context is the lens that separates them.

items.prompt: Audience awareness changes which of these?
choices: The numbers that are reported to each reader
The real cause behind the shortfall in sales
What is foregrounded and how much detail is given
items.explanation: Calibration shifts emphasis and detail. The facts themselves never change.

items.prompt: Which of these would be spin?
choices: Telling the principal 'the trip is on track' with the real total
Telling the principal 'we hit our goal' when you raised $340 of $500
Leaving out table-by-table details the principal cannot use
items.explanation: Spin creates an impression the facts do not support. The false 'hit our goal' does; the other two are true and relevant.

items.prompt: Is leaving out irrelevant detail the same as hiding the truth?
choices: No, omitting detail the reader does not need is not deception
Yes, any omission at all counts as hiding the truth from them
Yes, but only when the reader happens to be a decision-maker
items.explanation: Deception means hiding something the reader needs for their decision. Dropping irrelevant detail is just editing.

items.prompt: What is a 'load-bearing' detail?
choices: A detail that happens to be true and well known
A detail that the writer finds the most interesting
A detail that would change what the reader does
items.explanation: Load-bearing means removing it would change the reader's decision or reaction.

items.prompt: Two readers get messages that differ in length and tone. When is this still honest?
choices: Only when both messages are exactly the same length
When every checkable claim agrees across both messages
Only when neither message mentions any number at all
items.explanation: Different emphasis is fine as long as no claim would contradict the other message.

items.prompt: What happens to a number when you tailor a message?
choices: It stays identical for every reader
It is rounded in whichever direction sounds best
It is shown only to readers who ask for it
items.explanation: Numbers belong to the facts, and the facts do not change by audience.

items.prompt: Which word names changing what you put first for a reader?
choices: Fabricating
Contradicting
Foregrounding
items.explanation: Foregrounding is choosing what leads. It is legitimate, unlike changing the facts.

items.prompt: The principal hears only 'weather' as the cause. Is that spin?
choices: Yes, because every cause must always be given in full
No, it is true and enough for what the principal decides
Yes, because 'weather' is a vague word to use
items.explanation: 'Weather' is accurate and sufficient for a reader whose only question is whether the trip is on.

items.prompt: Priya tells her mother 'I got a B' and tells her friend 'the test was brutal, I got a B and half the class failed.' Is this audience awareness or spin?
choices: Spin, since her mother heard less than her friend did about it
Spin, since two different sentences were used for the two
Spin, since her friend heard a detail her mother never did
Audience awareness, since the grade matches and the rest is true
items.explanation: Both readers hear the same grade. Different detail is calibration as long as nothing contradicts.
items.reference:
Changes

Foregrounding, detail, the ask

Never changes

The actual facts

Why: adjusting emphasis for a reader is calibration; adjusting the facts themselves is deception.
items.learnMore:
What's allowed to change

Changes (calibration)

  • Foregrounding
  • Level of detail
  • The ask

Never changes (or it's deception)

  • The actual facts
  • The real timeline
  • The real cause

Two versions of the same update can look very different in tone and length while agreeing on every checkable claim.

Common mistake

The moment two versions would contradict each other if compared side by side, it's no longer audience awareness — it's incompatible stories, and it gets caught the first time two readers compare notes.
items.reflection: Recall a time you left something out for someone's benefit. Was it detail they did not need, or a truth they needed? How could you tell?

items.prompt: A volunteer tells the organizer 'we are fine on food' while telling a friend 'we may run short by 6pm.' What is the problem?
choices: Nothing, since each reader got a version suited to them
The friend should not have received any detail at all
The claims conflict, so this is two incompatible stories
The organizer should have heard the friend's version as well
items.explanation: Tailoring never changes the truth. When two versions would contradict each other side by side, it is no longer audience awareness.

Calibration changes emphasis; deception changes or hides needed truth
Calibration is spoken aloud; deception is always put in writing
Calibration is done by experts; deception is done by beginners
items.explanation: The test is what happens to the truth the reader needs, not the length or the medium.

items.prompt: What does a message written with no audience in mind usually default to?
choices: The writer's own frame
The reader's own frame
A neutral frame that suits everyone
items.explanation: Without a deliberate choice, the writer reverts to their own context and vocabulary.

items.prompt: The writer's default frame tends to be which kind of version?
choices: The shortest and most decision-oriented one available
The most formal and least detailed version possible
The most detailed and least decision-oriented one
items.explanation: Writers know the most about their own story, so unfiltered drafts tend to be long on detail and short on what the reader should do.

items.prompt: Which is one of the three questions to ask before writing?
choices: How many sentences can I fit into this one message?
What do they already know, and what do they need?
Which words will sound the most impressive to them?
items.explanation: The first question separates what is redundant from what is genuinely missing.

items.prompt: Which question settles what the message is asking of the reader?
choices: What decision or reaction am I trying to produce?
What time of day is the best to send it out?
How much did I enjoy writing this particular note?
items.explanation: Even informational messages carry an implicit ask, such as 'be aware' or 'no action needed'.

items.prompt: Which question tells you what has to be stated rather than implied?
choices: Who else might end up reading this note later on?
What is the nicest possible greeting to open with?
What will they misread if I don't address it?
items.explanation: Anticipating the likely misreading shows what must be said outright.

items.prompt: When is the best moment to name your reader?
choices: After the whole draft is finished
Before writing the first sentence
Only after someone complains about it
items.explanation: Choosing the reader upstream shapes content. Polishing afterward cannot fix a draft built around the wrong frame.

items.prompt: What does failing to adjust to the reader cost beyond clarity?
choices: Credibility
Money
Time zones
items.explanation: A speaker who ignores who is in the room seems not to understand the room, however correct the content.

items.prompt: Explaining a topic in identical words to a seven-year-old and to a room of adults mainly shows what?
choices: A deep respect for everyone equally
A gift for simple explanations
A failure to read the room
items.explanation: The issue is not intelligence or respect. Different listeners are deciding different things, so one version cannot fit both.

items.prompt: You write a long, thorough note to your landlord about a leaking tap, narrating every attempt you made. The landlord replies 'So what do you need from me?' Which question did your draft skip?
choices: What decision or reaction I wanted from the landlord
What time of day the tap first started leaking
Whether the landlord generally enjoys long messages
Which tools you used for each repair attempt
items.explanation: The note was written from the writer's frame, full of detail and with no clear ask. The ask question would have put 'please send a plumber' first.

You wrote from your own frame, not the friend's question
items.explanation: Unfiltered writing defaults to the writer's most detailed version. The friend probably wanted the highlights.

items.prompt: Which fix addresses a draft that serves the writer rather than the reader?

Add more detail so no reader can say it was incomplete
Name the reader and their question before rewriting the draft
Delete the draft and send a message that is only one word
items.explanation: The fix is upstream: decide who is reading and what they must settle, then rebuild. Polish and extra detail leave the wrong frame in place.

items.prompt: In the filter model, what stays identical across the groupmate, teacher, and principal versions?
choices: The amount of detail
The underlying facts
The opening sentence
items.explanation: One shared set of facts goes into the filter. Only the selection and emphasis differ.

items.prompt: In the filter model, what does the audience filter decide?
choices: Which facts are load-bearing for that reader
Which facts are true for that reader
Which facts the writer happens to remember
items.explanation: The filter selects what matters to a reader's decision. It never alters truth.

items.prompt: How many fact sources feed the three versions?
choices: Three, one per reader
Two, one casual and one formal
One
items.explanation: A single set of facts is projected three ways. Three separate sources would be three separate stories.

items.prompt: Is a detail load-bearing because of what it is, or because of who is reading?
choices: Because of how interesting the detail is to tell
Because of who is reading and what they decide
Because of how recently the detail happened
items.explanation: Load-bearing is defined relative to a reader's decision, not as a property of the fact alone.

items.prompt: Which detail is load-bearing for the principal?
choices: The trip is on track
Where the rain fell on the tables
How many cupcakes sold in the first hour
items.explanation: The principal's decision is whether the trip is still on, so that is the detail that changes what they do.

items.prompt: Which detail is load-bearing for the groupmate planning Saturday?
choices: That the school leadership was informed
That the trip is still on track
How the rain cut selling time in half
items.explanation: The groupmate can use the mechanism to plan a better Saturday. The principal's concerns do not help them.

items.prompt: What do the groupmate, teacher, and principal versions have in common in the filter diagram?
choices: They are all the same length
They come from the same set of facts
They all start with the same sentence
items.explanation: They differ in selection and emphasis, not in source.

items.prompt: A true fact that is irrelevant to a reader's stake is best called what?
choices: Noise for that reader
A lie to that reader
A decision for that reader
items.explanation: It is true, but it does not bear on what they need to settle, so it adds clutter rather than information.

items.prompt: A club treasurer reports the same budget to the members, the auditor, and a new volunteer. Which description matches the filter model?
choices: Three different sets of numbers, one tuned to each person
One set of numbers, with different details foregrounded for each
One identical document, since fairness means no differences
One set of numbers where every detail is repeated for everyone
items.explanation: The facts are shared. The filter changes which are foregrounded, such as totals for members, receipts for the auditor, and basics for the volunteer.

items.reflection: Take one recent event from your week. What would you keep and what would you cut if you told it to a close friend versus a stranger?

items.prompt: What does the groupmate already know that the principal does not?
choices: The final trip budget
The school's rules for fundraising
What happened at the table
items.explanation: The groupmate was there, so they hold table-level context. The principal knows nothing operational.

items.prompt: What does the teacher know that the groupmate may not?
choices: What the rain did to foot traffic
The goal and the deadline
Who bought which treats
items.explanation: The teacher operates at the commitment level: the $500 goal and when it is needed.

items.prompt: What does the principal know about how the sale ran?
choices: Almost nothing
Everything, since they approve events
Only the cause of the rain
items.explanation: The principal hears about it secondhand, so the message must work with outcome-level context.

items.prompt: What is the teacher's incentive in this story?
choices: Selling the most cupcakes
Moving the sale outdoors again
Hitting $500 in time
items.explanation: The teacher is accountable for the money, so that is what they fixate on.

items.prompt: What does the principal care about most?
choices: How the tables were arranged
Whether the trip is on
Who ran the cash box
items.explanation: The principal's stake is the trip itself, nothing operational.

items.prompt: What does the groupmate want from the message?
choices: To make Saturday go better
To know whether the principal approves
To find out the final trip budget
items.explanation: The groupmate is practical and forward-looking: they want what helps Saturday.

items.prompt: In the lens table, 'context' means what?
choices: How polite the reader expects the writer to be in tone
How long the message is allowed to run in total
The layer of the situation the reader already stands on
items.explanation: Context is identifying the layer a reader already stands on, such as table, commitment, or outcome.

items.prompt: Which channel fits a message to your groupmate best?
choices: A formal announcement
A quick informal text or word
A written report with headings
items.explanation: A groupmate shares context and expects casual communication.

items.prompt: A school sends one message about a cancelled field trip to parents, teachers, and students. Which pairing of reader and likely first question is best?
choices: Students: who signed off on the cancellation form?
Teachers: how much did the bus company charge us?
Parents: do I need to arrange childcare that day?
Parents: what lesson was the trip meant to teach?
items.explanation: Each group's stake produces a different first question. Parents are responsible for where their children are, so that is what they need settled before anything else.

items.prompt: When should a message lead with its conclusion?
choices: When the reader has little context and little time
Whenever the writer happens to feel nervous about it
Only when the message itself is very long indeed
items.explanation: Leading with the bottom line matters more the less context and time the reader has invested.

items.prompt: Which reader benefits most from a bottom-line-first message?
choices: The groupmate chatting in a text thread
The writer's own notes to themselves
The principal reading a cold update
items.explanation: A cold, first-touch reader needs the answer before anything else.

items.prompt: Why does a groupmate text not need the conclusion first?
choices: They are less intelligent than the principal
They share context, so detail can come first
They dislike short messages
items.explanation: Shared context makes a slower, conversational build natural.

items.prompt: What happens if the principal has to read three sentences before learning whether the trip is on?
choices: They start worrying before reaching the answer
They feel calmer thanks to the extra detail given
They skim it quickly and always guess correctly
items.explanation: A reader who has a pressing question is anxious until it is answered.

items.prompt: Is leading with the conclusion a rule for every channel?
choices: Yes, in every message no matter the reader
Yes, but only in written messages
No, it depends on the reader's context and time
items.explanation: It is a response to how much context and time a reader has, not a universal formatting rule.

items.prompt: What does forcing bottom-line-first onto a shared-context chat tend to do?
choices: It reads as warmer and kinder
It reads as stilted
It makes the chat shorter and clearer
items.explanation: Between people who share context, a rigid conclusion-first format can sound mechanical.

items.prompt: What does burying the point in a cold update tend to do?
choices: It reads as evasive and loses the reader
It reads as polite and careful
It makes the reader trust the writer more
items.explanation: A reader who cannot find the point soon often assumes something is being hidden.

items.prompt: Bottom-line-first is mostly about whose attention?
choices: The writer's reputation
The message's word count
The reader's attention
items.explanation: It is about the reader's limited attention, not their intelligence.

items.prompt: Your coach has two minutes between games. Which message to the coach is best?
choices: 'First, some background on how practice went on Tuesday...'
'Let me tell you about everyone's availability in order.'
'I have a few thoughts, and I'll build up to the one that matters.'
'Two players are out, so I'd start Jo at goalie. Okay?'
items.explanation: A time-pressed reader with little context gets the conclusion and ask first, with detail available on request.

items.prompt: What happens when you give the principal groupmate-level detail?
choices: They feel fully informed and quite calm afterward
They struggle to find the point and begin to worry
They ask for even more detail to be sent over
items.explanation: Too much detail buries the point. A reader who cannot find the answer starts to fear the answer is bad.

items.prompt: What happens when you give the groupmate principal-level brevity?
choices: They lack the detail needed and must ask you back
They get all of the detail they need to help
They stop caring about how Saturday goes at all
items.explanation: Too little detail forces a round-trip.

items.prompt: What does the teacher conclude from a message with no clear next step?
choices: That the situation is fully under control
That no response is needed
That you may not have a plan
items.explanation: Missing next steps read as missing thinking, not just unclear news.

items.prompt: What does a vague reassurance with no number do to the principal's trust?
choices: It builds trust through a confident tone
It erodes trust before the real update lands
It makes no difference to their trust either way
items.explanation: Without anything checkable, reassurance feels like a dodge.

items.prompt: Is the goal to always add more detail?
choices: No, it is to match detail to each reader
Yes, since more detail is always the safer option
Yes, but only for readers who are in charge
items.explanation: Both over-detail and under-detail fail. The aim is matching, not a universal direction.

items.prompt: Is the goal to always trim detail?
choices: Yes, since shorter is always clearer for readers
Yes, whenever the writer happens to be busy
No, some readers need the detail to act
items.explanation: Trimming strips what a close-up reader may need.

items.prompt: Which mismatch costs you an extra round-trip?
choices: Too much detail for a reader who does not
Too little detail for a reader who needs it
A vague reassurance sent to a distant reader
items.explanation: When the reader is missing something they need to act, they must come back to ask.

items.prompt: Which mismatch makes a reader escalate worriedly?
choices: Burying a distant reader in operational detail
Giving a close-up reader the full story
Giving a close-up reader a clear next step
items.explanation: A distant reader who cannot find the point worries and asks whether everything is okay.

items.prompt: You tell your sister who is hosting a dinner 'Everything's fine!' without saying whether you can bring dessert. What is the most likely cost?
choices: She must come back and ask what you are bringing
She trusts you more because you stayed so positive
She plans around the dessert without ever asking
She assumes you are bringing nothing at all
items.explanation: The missing specific detail forces an extra exchange.

items.prompt: How many questions does the decision procedure ask?
choices: Two
Seven
Four
items.explanation: The four questions are: what do they know, what are they measured on, what do I need from them, and should the conclusion lead.

items.prompt: What is the first question in the decision procedure?
choices: Should the conclusion come first?
What does this audience already know?
What decision do I need?
items.explanation: Start with what the audience already holds, so you do not re-explain it.

items.prompt: What is the second question?
choices: What are they actually measured on?
How long should this be?
Which channel is easiest for me?
items.explanation: Their stake filters the facts down to the ones that bear on it.

items.prompt: What is the third question?
choices: How long should the whole message end up being?
How can I make the message sound impressive?
What decision or reaction do I need from them?
items.explanation: This is the ask, even when the ask is just 'be aware'.

items.prompt: What is the fourth question?
choices: Which words in the message are the rarest ones?
Does this channel expect the bottom line first?
Who else on the team should be copied in?
items.explanation: This question decides whether the ask leads or trails.

items.prompt: Which questions decide the content of the message?
choices: The first three
Only the fourth
None of them
items.explanation: Questions one to three decide content; the fourth is placement.

items.prompt: Which question is only about arrangement?
choices: The first, about what the audience already knows
The third, about the decision that is needed
The fourth, whether to lead with the conclusion
items.explanation: The fourth cannot be answered before the content exists.

items.prompt: Is the procedure a formula or a consistent habit?
choices: A formula that outputs the exact wording
A habit of asking the same questions in order
A rule that only applies to teachers
items.explanation: It is not a template. It is the same questions applied each time instead of improvised.

items.prompt: A friend skips question 3 and writes a long, accurate account of a missed flight to their boss. The boss replies 'So what do you need?' What should the friend have settled first?
choices: Whether the boss prefers formal or casual wording
The decision or reaction they wanted from the boss
How many details about the airport to include
Whether the boss reads messages before or after lunch
items.explanation: Question 3 produces the ask. Without it the message is information with no purpose.
items.reference:
① What do they know?
② What are they measured on?
③ What decision do I need?
④ Bottom line first, or trailing?

Why: the first three decide the content; the fourth is a placement decision that depends on already having that content.

items.prompt: Why can question 4 not be answered before question 3?

Because the channel is not known until the ask is sent
Because the fourth question is the least important one

items.explanation: You cannot decide whether to lead with the ask until you know what it is.

items.prompt: Which reader gets the version with the most operational specifics?
choices: The groupmate who ran the table
The teacher who counts on the money
The principal who hears it secondhand
items.explanation: The groupmate was there and can use the mechanism to plan Saturday, so their version carries the most detail.

items.prompt: Which reader gets only the outcome and the timeline?
choices: The groupmate
The teacher
The principal
items.explanation: The principal's only questions are whether the trip is on and when they will know for sure.

items.prompt: What does the teacher version foreground?
choices: The exact way the rain disrupted the tables
Whether the $500 goal is still reachable in time
The principal's reaction
items.explanation: The teacher is accountable for the money, so that is answered first.

items.prompt: How does the teacher version phrase its ask?
choices: As a clear default with an easy override
As an open-ended request for new ideas
As a formal request for written approval
items.explanation: 'I'll run it as planned unless you say otherwise' gives a busy reader a quick yes or no.

items.prompt: Does the groupmate version need a formal ask?
choices: Yes, a formal request for their approval
Yes, a firm deadline for them to reply by
No, only something to do if Saturday needs help
items.explanation: Groupmates do not need to be asked to note something; they are told what to do if anything is needed.

items.prompt: The teacher version is longer than the groupmate version. What does it spend the extra words on?
choices: More detail on the rain
The trade-off and the default
Greetings and thanks
items.explanation: Word count tracks how much a version explains its reasoning and ask, not how much operational detail it has.

items.prompt: What is the principal version's cause for the shortfall?
choices: Just 'weather'
The full story of the rain and tables
No cause is given at all
items.explanation: It is true and sufficient for what the principal decides.

items.prompt: Which version lets the groupmate help plan Saturday better?
choices: The one giving only the final outcome and nothing else
The one giving only the new date for Saturday
The one naming fewer tables and less traffic
items.explanation: The mechanism is what a groupmate can act on.

items.prompt: A student tells their coach about a missed practice. The coach is balancing a dozen players and needs a fast reply. Which version fits the teacher pattern best?
choices: 'I missed Tuesday. Long story involving my sibling, my car, the weather, and a very long afternoon.'
'I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm so sorry about Tuesday, please let me know exactly how to make it right.'
'I missed Tuesday due to a sick sibling. I'll make up the drills Thursday unless you prefer another time.'
'Just so you know, Tuesday did not work out for me.'
items.explanation: A clear status, a plan, and an easy default with an override respect a busy reader's time.

items.prompt: Is the groupmate version more honest than the principal version?
choices: Yes, because it contains so much more detail
No, both are honest and differ only in detail
Yes, because it was written before the others
items.explanation: Omitting irrelevant detail is not the same as omitting relevant detail.

items.prompt: What stays identical across all three versions?
choices: The numbers: $340 of $500 with a fix on Saturday
The length of each of the three messages
The opening line used in each of the messages
items.explanation: Different numbers per audience would be deception, and it gets caught when readers compare notes.

items.prompt: What does calibration mean?
choices: Changing the numbers to suit each reader
Making every message the same length
Changing emphasis without changing the truth
items.explanation: Calibration adjusts foregrounding and detail only.

items.prompt: What does deception mean in this unit?
choices: Leaving out any detail the reader does not need
Changing, hiding, or blurring a truth the reader needs
Choosing a shorter version for a busy reader
items.explanation: Deception targets what the reader needs in order to decide correctly.

items.prompt: What happens when two readers compare notes and the numbers differ?
choices: The writer loses credibility
Both readers feel better informed
The shorter message is trusted more
items.explanation: Different facts per audience get caught the moment readers compare.

items.prompt: Which constant is true for every version: answers that reader's real...?
choices: Word count
Opening greeting
'So what'
items.explanation: Each version answers what that reader actually wants to settle.

items.prompt: Dropping the rain details for the principal is an example of what?
choices: Hiding a relevant truth from them to avoid worry
Omitting detail that would not change their decision
Making up an entirely new cause for the shortfall
items.explanation: The detail is true but not load-bearing for the principal.

items.prompt: Which test best tells calibration from deception?
choices: Would the versions contradict each other side by side?
Which of the versions is the shorter of the two?
Which of the versions sounds the happier one?
items.explanation: If every checkable claim agrees, the versions are calibrated. A contradiction means deception.

items.prompt: Lena tells her parents she scored 70% on a quiz and tells her friend 'I did okay.' Is the reply to her friend deception?
choices: Yes, since any shortened version of a number is deception
No, since friends are never owed a number of any kind
Yes, since a friend can never be told less than a parent
No, nothing false was said, but nothing checkable was given
items.explanation: 'I did okay' contradicts nothing, so it is not deception. It is a weaker message, because the friend wanted something concrete and got a vague reply. Calibration still keeps the real number available.
items.reference:
✅ No version contains a false claim
✅ The actual numbers are identical in all three
✅ Every version answers that reader's "so what"

Why: omitting irrelevant detail isn't the same as omitting relevant detail — that's the line between calibration and deception.
items.learnMore:
The three constants, checked
ConstantWhy it matters
No contradicting claims across versionsOtherwise it's not calibration, it's different stories
Concrete numbers identical everywhereA number that varies by audience is the deception line
Every version answers that reader's real 'so what'Not a generic summary that technically mentions the topic

Common mistake

Assuming detail-level differences mean the versions are inconsistent. They're not, as long as all three constants above hold.
items.reflection: Where is your own line between simplifying something for someone and hiding something they needed? What would tell you that you had crossed it?

items.prompt: A store manager tells staff 'sales dipped slightly' and tells the owner 'sales fell 12%' about the same week. Which reading is most reasonable?
choices: That is calibration, since staff need less detail overall
That is fine, since owners always want to see big numbers
Likely deception, since the sizes of the drop conflict
That is fine, since 'slightly' is a matter of opinion
items.explanation: 'Slightly' and '12%' make different claims about the same fact. Calibration would keep the number and vary emphasis, not the size.

items.prompt: A guide tells nervous hikers 'the trail is rough but well-marked' and never mentions that the last mile needs scrambling, which they would need to know before deciding to go. Is that calibration?
choices: Yes, since the hikers heard a true and shorter version
No, it hides a truth the nervous group needs to decide
Yes, since nervous hikers should always hear gentler wording
Yes, since experienced hikers heard the scramble anyway
items.explanation: Calibration changes emphasis. It does not withhold a fact the reader needs for their decision. The scramble is exactly that kind of fact for people deciding whether to go.

items.prompt: What goes wrong when you give the principal the groupmate version?
choices: They gain a deep appreciation of all the detail
They end up trusting the writer a great deal more
They can't find the point and may fear a problem
items.explanation: Full detail with no clear ask reads as confusing or like burying the point.

items.prompt: What goes wrong when you give the groupmate the principal version?
choices: They feel overloaded with too many specifics
They are missing the detail needed to help
They are annoyed by the polite tone of it
items.explanation: The failure is symmetric: stripped detail leaves a close reader unable to act.

items.prompt: Is 'no detail' the same as 'no substance'?
choices: No, you can cut jargon but keep the real number
Yes, cutting detail always removes substance
Yes, and that is why short messages fail
items.explanation: '$340 of $500, fixed Saturday' is short but still checkable.

items.prompt: What is wrong with 'just so you know...' and no next step?
choices: It is far too polite a tone for a teacher
It contains too many facts for the reader
The reader cannot tell what reaction is wanted
items.explanation: Burying or skipping the ask leaves the reader unsure whether to act.

items.prompt: What is the fix for a buried ask?
choices: Add three more paragraphs of context
State a default plus an easy override
Remove all numbers
items.explanation: As in the teacher version: say what you will do and let them redirect you.

items.prompt: Is there a single safe direction: always more detail or always less?
choices: No, both directions are real failures to avoid
Yes, the safe direction is always more detail
Yes, the safe direction is always less detail
items.explanation: The fix is matching detail to the reader.

items.prompt: What does a vague reassurance with no checkable claim signal?
choices: Great confidence on the part of the writer
A very respectful and careful tone overall
Possible evasion, since nothing can be verified
items.explanation: A claim the reader can check builds trust; vagueness does not.

items.prompt: Which is a failure mode listed for this unit?
choices: Using the same true numbers when writing to every reader
Giving a short version only because of someone's title
Offering a clear default along with an easy override
items.explanation: Over-indexing on role instead of stake is a listed failure.

items.prompt: Nadia writes her landlord a short note saying 'Things are handled.' The landlord needs to know whether the repair date is firm. What failure is this?
choices: Cutting detail so far that nothing checkable remains
Giving too much detail to a distant reader
Using the groupmate pattern on the wrong reader
Adding too many technical terms for a non-expert reader
items.explanation: Short is fine; empty is not. A date or a plain status would have kept the message brief and still useful.
items.reference:
Groupmate version → principal
Can't find the point
Principal version → groupmate
Missing detail to help

Why: the failure is symmetric — matching detail to the reader is the goal, not minimizing it for everyone.
items.learnMore:
The failure is symmetric

Groupmate version → principal

  • Can't find the point
  • Assumes something's wrong

Principal version → groupmate

  • Missing detail to help
  • Forces a round-trip

Common mistake

Picking one direction as the 'safe default' (always more detail, or always less). Both directions are real failures — the fix is matching, not a universal bias.
items.reflection: Which of the failure modes do you slip into most often, and what small habit would catch it before you send?

items.prompt: An organizer sends a thrilled, detailed letter about the new schedule to a volunteer who only needed to know their shift time. Which failure fits best?
choices: Principal-level brevity sent to a close collaborator
A missing ask sent to an overloaded and busy reader
A vague reassurance sent to a distant reader
Groupmate-level detail sent to a reader who needs the bottom line
items.explanation: The reader needed a single fact and was given a story to dig through.

items.prompt: Which rewrite best repairs 'Just flagging, the shipment might be delayed'?
choices: 'The shipment might be delayed, and delays often happen for many reasons including weather.'
'Please be aware that the shipment may be delayed, and I apologize for any inconvenience this may cause.'
'The shipment is likely two days late. I'll confirm tomorrow unless you'd rather I reroute it.'
'Hi, quick note: re the shipment, there might be something going on, let me know.'
items.explanation: The rewrite adds a checkable claim, a plan, and a default with an override. The alternatives add words without adding the ask.

Can't find the point
Principal version → groupmate
Missing detail to help

items.prompt: Which is a better guide to what a reader needs: their title or their question?
choices: Their question and what they are measured on
Their title alone, whatever they happen to ask
How loudly they tend to speak in meetings
items.explanation: A title predicts context and stake on average. The question in front of you is direct evidence.

items.prompt: The principal asks, 'How many tables did you have?' What do you answer with?
choices: Only 'the trip is on track'
A reminder to read the earlier note
The number of tables
items.explanation: A specific question asks for the specific answer, regardless of who is asking.

items.prompt: What does a narrow, detailed question signal?
choices: That the asker wants a short reply
That the asker wants a detailed answer
That the asker does not care about the topic
items.explanation: The question itself is the best guide to what they want.

items.prompt: What is the danger of using a title-based lookup table?
choices: It ignores what the reader is actually asking
It shows the reader far too much respect
It makes every message much longer than needed
items.explanation: A lookup like 'leaders get short, others get long' misfires when the question says otherwise.

items.prompt: The principal version is short. Does that mean the principal always gets short answers?
choices: Yes, always
Yes, because principals dislike detail
No, only when the question is the broad one
items.explanation: The short version fits the question 'is the trip on?'. A narrow question needs a narrow, detailed answer.

items.prompt: What should override a title-based guess?
choices: Your own mood on the day you write it
A specific question the reader asks
The length of the draft you have written
items.explanation: Evidence from the reader beats a general assumption.

items.prompt: Giving 'the trip is on track' to a principal who asked for table counts is what kind of answer?
choices: Evasive
Perfectly calibrated
Overly detailed
items.explanation: It dodges the question asked.

items.prompt: Which two things does the lens actually track?
choices: The reader's title and their approximate age
The writer's mood and the time of day they write
The question asked and what the reader is judged on
items.explanation: These are the real signals of stake. Title is just a shortcut.

items.prompt: A school secretary, usually brief, asks you for the exact room number and time of the meeting. Which reply fits?
choices: 'It's all in the schedule I sent, but it's on track.'
'A few details are still being worked out, so check back.'
'Room 14, 3:30pm, and here is how we chose it, step by step.'
items.explanation: A narrow question wants a narrow, exact answer, however brief the asker usually is.
items.reference:
🎭 Role
≠
🎯 Stake (what they're actually asking + measured on)

Why: someone asking a specific, detailed question is signaling they want the detailed answer — regardless of title.

items.reflection: Think of someone you assume wants the short version because of their role. What question could you ask or listen for to check that assumption?

items.prompt: A CEO of a bakery asks the new hire, 'Walk me through why the batch failed.' A coworker advises giving only a one-line summary because 'CEOs hate detail.' What is wrong with the advice?

It is correct, since the title predicts what executives want
It gives the CEO too many facts
It asks the new hire to be less honest with the CEO
items.explanation: The request for a walkthrough is direct evidence of what the reader wants.

items.prompt: When is a short, outcome-only reply the right choice for a busy leader?
choices: Whenever their title is high, whatever they ask you
Whenever you are short on time before the meeting
Whenever the news is good rather than bad
When their question is broad, such as 'is the plan on?'
items.explanation: Fit the answer to the question, not to the rank. A broad question gets the broad answer.
